nameStory: The 'rusty' in Rusty Foxglove comes from its distinctive rust-colored flowers that bloom along tall spikes in summer. The scientific name 'ferruginea' literally means 'rusty colored' in Latin, referring to that warm, reddish-brown hue that makes this foxglove stand out from its more commonly seen purple cousins.
description: Rusty Foxglove is a tall, stately plant that can reach up to 4 feet in height, making it quite the garden showstopper. It starts as a low rosette of dark green, oblong leaves in its first year, then sends up impressive spikes of tubular, rust-colored flowers in its second year. This European native is rarely seen growing wild in New England, with only a couple of documented sightings, but it occasionally appears in gardens where it has escaped cultivation.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive rust or reddish-brown tubular flowers arranged in tall, dense spikes. Each flower is about an inch long with a slightly flared opening, and they have a papery, almost metallic texture when you look closely.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green, oblong leaves that form a basal rosette in the first year. The leaves feel slightly rough and have prominent veins running lengthwise from base to tip.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a biennial, forming a low leaf rosette the first year, then shooting up a tall flowering spike (3-4 feet) in the second year before dying.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: The flowering stem is sturdy and unbranched, rising straight up from the center of the leaf rosette with a slightly fuzzy texture.

habitat: In New England, Rusty Foxglove is extremely rare and typically found only where it has escaped from cultivation near old gardens or homesteads. When it does establish, it prefers well-drained soils in partial shade to full sun, often along woodland edges or disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the basal rosette, with fresh leaves unfurling. First-year plants remain as ground-hugging rosettes.
seasonality.summer: Spectacular bloom time! The tall rust-colored flower spikes are at their peak, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop. Second-year plants begin to decline after setting seed.
seasonality.winter: First-year rosettes may persist under snow cover, while second-year plants die back completely, leaving only seeds for the next generation.

funFact: Despite being called 'rusty,' this foxglove's unique color comes from the same type of compounds that give autumn leaves their brilliant oranges and browns - it's literally wearing fall colors all summer long!
confusionNotes: The rust-colored flowers make this nearly impossible to confuse with other foxgloves in New England, since Purple Foxglove has pink-purple blooms. The main confusion might be with other tall spiky wildflowers, but no other plant has quite this distinctive rusty-brown tubular flower arrangement.
contextualKnowledge: Like all foxgloves, every part of this plant is highly toxic and can cause serious illness if eaten. Even handling the leaves can cause skin reactions in sensitive people, so admire from a distance and always wash hands after any contact.
compareHints: Among the foxglove family, Rusty Foxglove is unique for its rust-brown flowers - Purple Foxglove has pink-purple blooms, while Yellow Foxglove (rarely seen here) has pale yellow flowers. The flower color is really the dead giveaway, since all foxgloves share that distinctive tubular flower shape and tall spike arrangement.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple foxglove is the most common foxglove species in New England and the most likely to naturalize from gardens.
Yellow foxglove stands out from its more common cousin, purple foxglove, by its soft yellow color and larger individual blooms.

Among foxgloves in New England, straw foxglove is distinguished by its pale, cream-yellow flowers that are much smaller and more numerous than the large, bright yellow blooms of yellow foxglove (Digitalis grandiflora).
Woolly foxglove stands out from other foxgloves by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves and small, densely-packed cream flowers.
